newsitem.title: UK: City split on UK govt plans to control gilt sales.
newsitem.headline: City split on UK govt plans to control gilt sales.

text.p: Aficionados of the British gilt market were sharply divided on Tuesday about the implications of the government's plans to take control of debt issuance from the Bank of England.

Some said it was fraught with danger while others dismissed it as mere tweaking of a sometimes arcane market in order to complete reforms begun in earnest four years ago. The idea of taking control of gilt issuance away from the central bank was first mooted as part of that process while the Conservatives were still in power.

"Whatever happens, the authorities should continue in their agenda of reform to the gilt market," said Jim Leaviss on the fixed income desk at M&G Investment Management. "Around 90 percent of that's been done already, we've now got 90 percent of a great bond market, but it still needs a few little tweaks."

The Treasury said on Tuesday it would work on detailed proposals for its new role in charge of debt issuance in consultation with gilt market participants and the Bank of England. It said it aimed to finalise the proposals by July to be implemented as soon as feasible after that.
The move was first announced last week when Chancellor Gordon Brown handed control of interest rates over to the Bank of England. The Bank had only one day's notice of the wide-ranging changes.
Leaviss said it made little difference whether the Bank of England or the Treasury was in control of debt management -- but noted the Bank had a wealth of expertise on which to draw.
He said the main thing was to have a transparent, inflexible system of debt issuance.

Some analysts said the decision to wrench control of debt management from the Bank was designed to eliminate any potential conflict of interest between the setting of monetary policy and decisions on debt issuance.
"That was the reason given on the day the government announced it was handing control of interest rates to the Bank," said one gilt edged market maker.

"Another thing is that the Treasury is clearly keen to conform to international practice, and maybe this makes the gilt market more recognisable to international investors -- it's another step along the long road of reform since 1993."
But others suggested an ulteria motive behind the move, saying the decision was steeped in politics.

"There is a history of disgruntlement in the Treasury about the way the Bank handles the gilt market and it has long felt the Bank has dragged its heels over reform of the gilt market," said one City expert.
He said morale in the Treasury was low as first they lost their prestigious Whitehall building, then control of interest rates. "This was a quid pro quo, a political decision," he said.
He said the idea it eliminated any potential conflict of interest in setting monetary policy and controlling Britain's debt was a complete non-starter.
"That's nonsense. The Bank has to set out its quarterly funding schedule in advance. There's little room for messing around," he said.

And as for the argument that the move brings Britain into line with other major economies, the expert noted that the Bundesbank -- the mother of all central banks -- issues all German government debt and controls the market.
Analysts suggested that Treasury control of debt management could also introduce a whole new round of political speculation.

For instance, if the Treasury issued a disproportionate amount of gilts early in a financial year, speculation may rise about possible policy initiatives harmful to the gilt market, later in the year -- tax cuts or plans to increase spending, perhaps.
The reverse would also apply. A slow start to gilt issuance could spark rumours of tight spending plans, leading to a lower-than-expected PSBR.
Whatever the implications of Brown's plans, one trader said the Bank of England "was hopping mad" about being robbed of one of its traditional roles.
But the Bank would offer no comment either way.
